Name of patient: Rogers, Pamela

---

Heading: Symptoms and Descriptions

Symptom 1: Chest Pain
Description: Dull and aching in character, beginning in the left para-sternal area and radiating up to the neck. First episode occurred during physical exertion (gardening) approximately one week prior to admission, lasting 5 to 10 minutes and resolving with rest. Two additional episodes followed: one lasting 15 minutes while walking the dog (resolved with rest), and one episode that awoke the patient from sleep lasting 30 minutes, prompting the Emergency Department visit. Pain is increasing in frequency and duration, with no relief attempted other than rest. No association with movement, food, or palpation. The pattern is consistent with unstable angina.

Symptom 2: Dyspnea / Shortness of Breath
Description: The patient becomes short of breath during chest pain episodes. No other exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is reported outside of these episodes. Physical examination findings of a third heart sound and bilateral pulmonary crackles at the lung bases suggest possible left ventricular dysfunction and congestive heart failure secondary to myocardial ischemia.

Symptom 3: Epigastric Pain
Description: Burning in quality, occurring approximately twice a month, noticed primarily at night. The patient has a prior history of peptic ulcer disease and currently uses OTC ibuprofen (Advil) on a near-daily basis, which may be a contributing factor.

Symptom 4: Lower Back Pain
Description: Aching in quality, occurring approximately once every week, typically after working in the garden. Usually relieved with Tylenol (acetaminophen). No other arthralgias, muscle aches, or pains reported.

Symptom 5: Hypertension
Description: Diagnosed with hypertension in 1998 (approximately 3 years prior to admission). Previously placed on an unknown antihypertensive medication but stopped after 6 months due to drowsiness. Blood pressure on admission measured at 168/98, indicating currently uncontrolled hypertension. The combination of recent-onset hypertension and an abdominal bruit raises concern for a secondary cause, specifically renovascular hypertension due to atherosclerotic disease of the renal artery.

Symptom 6: Cystic Changes of the Breasts
Description: Cystic changes noted bilaterally on physical examination. No masses or nipple discharge observed. Consistent with fibrocystic breast disease.

---

Heading: Severity Report

Severity Report: #High
Reason: The severity is assessed as High based on multiple concerning clinical findings documented in the report. The patient's chest pain has progressively worsened over one week — increasing in frequency, duration, and now occurring at rest (nocturnal episode lasting 30 minutes), which is explicitly identified in the document as fitting the presentation of unstable angina, for which hospitalization is indicated. Additional high-risk findings include a blood pressure of 168/98 (uncontrolled hypertension), shortness of breath accompanied by a third heart sound and bilateral pulmonary crackles suggestive of left ventricular dysfunction and possible congestive heart failure, a systolic murmur radiating to the neck raising concern for aortic stenosis, and an abdominal bruit suggesting possible renovascular disease. The patient also carries multiple cardiovascular risk factors including family history of premature coronary artery disease (CAD), early surgical menopause without hormone replacement therapy, and uncontrolled hypertension. The clinical assessment in the document explicitly recommends hospital admission and urgent cardiac catheterization, further confirming the high severity of this case.
